---
title: "See the Pattern"
subtitle: "Why we draw data instead of staring at it"
toc: false
---

Spreadsheets are great for **storing** data and **looking up** a single value. They are terrible for **seeing patterns**. Our eyes and brains can only hold a handful of numbers at a time, but they can take in the shape of thousands of points at a glance.

Each page on this site runs the same little experiment:

1. **The spreadsheet.** You get the raw data, just like you'd receive it in a CSV.
2. **Your guess.** A question about the data. Try to answer it by scanning the table. Give yourself a minute (really!).
3. **The reveal.** Open the chart and see how long the same answer takes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
from sim_data import study_scores

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
df = study_scores()

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.3]})
ax1.axis("off")
cells = df.head(10)[["hours_studied", "exam_score"]].values
tbl = ax1.table(cellText=cells, colLabels=["hours", "score"], loc="center", cellLoc="center")
tbl.scale(1, 1.2)
ax1.set_title("10 of 150 rows…", fontsize=11)
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="hours_studied", y="exam_score", ax=ax2, s=25, color="#2a6f97")
ax2.set(title="…versus all 150 at once", xlabel="Hours studied", ylabel="Exam score")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
